transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-12
Start time (UTC): 16:00
Duration: ~57 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Omar Patel (Redwood SE), Elena Ruiz (Redwood CSM), Dana Morris (RetailBridge CTO), Carlos Jimenez (Lead Engineer), Priya Singh (Head of Infra), Aisha Khan (Security)

Summary:
Quick console-led walkthrough showing incident playback, request-to-trace correlation, error triage flow, and discussion around hosted vs dedicated for predictable tail latency. Customer wanted to see how to map request IDs back to model fallback paths and audit logs for compliance.

Topics covered:
- Request replay / playback in the Console
- Trace mapping and hop visualization
- KV cache fallback and model variant fallthrough
- Audit logs / KMS / SSO concerns
- Pilot and benchmarking next steps

Questions to answer during call:
- Can we reproduce the high tail latency seen last week?
- How do audit logs retain request payloads and where are they stored?
- What's the rollback behavior when a model variant fails?

--- Transcript ---
[00:00:00] Maya: alright everyone thanks for joining, uh quick intro — i'm Maya chen from Redwood, i'm the ae on this thread, with me is Omar our se and Elena on CSM.
[00:00:12] Dana: hey thanks, hi all. we wanted to walk through an actual incident we had last week where our checkout personalization calls spiked. we captured request ids and a couple of sample logs, hope that's ok.
[00:00:25] Maya: perfect, that's exactly what we want. you sent over three request ids right? carlos, can you confirm which ones we should load?
[00:00:33] Carlos: yeah — i dropped them in the chat: rb-req-1121, rb-req-1134, rb-req-1159. the 1159 is the one that timed out and triggered our retry cascade.
[00:00:44] Omar: great, i'll start by showing the console "Incident Replay" flow, we're going to take one request id and show how it stitches to the trace and the request logs — sometimes the auto-transcription in the console calls it "request playback" in the UI.
[00:00:58] [00:01:00] Omar: ok pulling up the Replay tab, so you can drop in an rb-req id, we parse headers, model variant, route and then surface the per-hop latencies — you can see the prefix cache hit rate, kv cash — sorry, kv cache, yeah — we see a miss on this one.
[00:01:18] Dana: ok that kv cache miss is interesting — our frontend is supposed to warm the cache on signup flow.
[00:01:24] Omar: right, on this request our trace shows a 480ms wait in the model queue and then a 1.2s decode — overall token time stacked. also note the fallback path — console annotates when we route to a cheaper quantized model versus the primary. on rb-req-1159 we actually have a model fallback at timestamp 2027-05-05T14:12:03Z.
[00:01:45] Carlos: can you show where that decision happens? i want to see if it's a capacity-based fallback or an explicit policy.
[00:01:51] Omar: yeah here — the trace node says "fallback_router: model_variant=v2-q4_approx, reason=latency_sla_breach". sometimes that reason string is a little terse; we'll paste the raw JSON in the followup.
[00:02:06] [00:02:15] Aisha: quick security question — when you say "raw JSON" does that include the request prompt? how is PII handled in these artifacts?
[00:02:23] Elena: good Q. our default is to redact prompt content in exports for hosted customers, we offer an opt-in full trace export for dedicated/private where you can control retention and KMS. i'll share the security pack with exact fields.
[00:02:36] Aisha: and that KMS integration, does it support customer-owned keys in AWS?
[00:02:41] Elena: yes — we support CMKs and HSM-backed keys, that's in the pack.
[00:02:46] [00:2:50] Priya: what about SSO + RBAC? we need SAML with SCIM provisioning and fine-grained roles.
[00:02:56] Maya: we integrate SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and console RBAC can be scoped to project/route/model. i'll attach the RBAC matrix.
[00:03:06] Omar: back to the trace: notice the long tail is at the decode stage. that's often the model or the quantization path choice. for reproducibility we have an "open in Request Inspector" button which opens the token timeline plus full event log.
[00:03:22] [00:03:30] Carlos: pull up the Request Inspector for 1159 please.
[00:03:33] Omar: doing that — here, token timeline on the left, event timeline on the right. see how there's a burst of small requests that preceded this one — looks like a burst from a batch job. our batching window could've grouped these causing queue contention.
[00:03:49] Carlos: that sounds like our scheduler — we run a small nightly batch around that hour. we didn't think it would impact personalization.
[00:03:55] Dana: so is the fix to change batching/window or do we need dedicated capacity?
[00:04:00] Maya: depends on your tolerance for tail latency. if you have strict SLOs (p95/p99) and unpredictable bursts, Dedicated with reserved GPU pools gives predictable tail. hosted can be tuned with conservative batching/always-warm routing rules but has shared capacity elements.
[00:04:15] [00:04:20] Priya: can you quantify cost delta for dedicated vs hosted for a profile like ours? we have ~2M tokens/day for personalization.
[00:04:28] Maya: we'll send a tailored estimate — rough rule: dedicated becomes cost-advantageish when you need consistent baseline throughput and want to avoid per-token burst tax. we'll include an Optimize profile that suggests batch sizes and model quantization to meet p99 targets.
[00:04:42] Omar: also worth noting: the Console's "fallback map" shows frequency of fallbacks by route — see this heatmap, you can filter by time-range and model variant.
[00:04:52] [00:05:00] Carlos: in this heatmap, can we click to see the raw traces that contributed?
[00:05:03] Omar: yes — click the cell and it lists request ids, then you can replay each one, or export a csv with timestamps and error flags.
[00:05:12] Dana: you mentioned audit logs earlier — what's the retention and what fields are in the audit?
[00:05:18] Elena: hosted customers get 90 days of full audit logs (meta only, prompts redacted). Dedicated can opt for longer retention or ship logs to a customer S3/GCS bucket; we can also forward to SIEMs via syslog/obs forwarder.
[00:05:31] Aisha: can we have logs forwarded to our Splunk instance?
[00:05:34] Elena: yes — we have connectors for Splunk and Datadog. we'll add the Splunk runbook link in the followup.
[00:05:40] [00:05:50] Maya: quick demo of error analysis: the Console surfaces "error fingerprints" — e.g. timeouts, decode-exceptions, quota-deny. you can group by fingerprint and drill into representative traces.
[00:05:59] Omar: showing grouping now — we've got 137 timeouts in that 6-hour spike, group shows a common precondition: all were routed through route "personalization-v3" and share a similar queue spike pattern.
[00:06:10] Carlos: ok so practically, what do we change — we can either: a) change our client-side retry/backoff b) adjust batching windows c) move to dedicated or d) pin model variants to avoid fallback.
[00:06:21] Dana: what's the impact of pinning models long term? we worried about quality drift.
[00:06:26] Omar: pinning prevents automatic fallback so you avoid surprises, but you lose the automatic capacity-based degradation benefit. you can do canary pinning for certain routes and monitor quality via the Console's eval hooks.
[00:06:36] [00:06:45] Priya: about the eval hooks — we already run nightly prompt sets to detect regressions, can we wire that into your rollout pipeline?
[00:06:51] Omar: yes, you can attach a prompt set to a rollout and we block a rollout if eval scores drop beyond threshold. we'll show a quick example in the pilot.
[00:07:00] [00:07:08] Carlos: back to the specific 1159 request — is there a human readable correlation between our logs and your trace id? our logs use X-Request-Id.
[00:07:15] Omar: yes we ingest request headers and store the X-Request-Id as "external_request_id" in the trace metadata — that's how the Replay finds it. sometimes the header is dropped by proxies, so worth checking.
[00:07:28] Carlos: thanks, we'll double-check at our edge.
[00:07:35] [00:07:40] Maya: i noticed in the trace there's an upstream call to a reranker — is that part of your stack? Carlos: yeah we call a small reranker service before hitting the model.
[00:07:47] Omar: that'll show up as a remote call in the hop map — you can click and see remote call latency and response status. in this case the reranker responded 200 but with a 300ms median which contributed to the overall latency.
[00:07:59] Dana: ok so multiple contributing factors. for the pilot we'd like to test two mitigations: 1) move personalization to a pinned high-q model for peak hours and 2) reserve 2-gpu dedicated pool for the window.
[00:08:12] Maya: sounds reasonable. Omar, can you outline what the pilot will look like?
[00:08:17] Omar: sure — we'll provision a small dedicated pool and an Optimize profile: set conservative batching window (20ms), pre-warm KV cache for the personalization prefix, pin model variant for peak hours and collect p95/p99 and token cost. we'll run for 72 hours with synthetic and live traffic.
[00:08:34] [00:08:40] Carlos: how do we setup the pre-warm? is there an API call?
[00:08:43] Omar: yes, the Console has a "warm prefixes" scheduler or you can call REST /v1/warm with a list of prompt prefixes. we'll include sample curl in the runbook.
[00:08:53] Aisha: as part of the pilot we need to validate that no prompts are stored unencrypted outside our KMS control.
[00:08:59] Elena: we will restrict full-text capture and use customer-managed KMS for any exports. also we can keep redaction on by default and enable full export only via a signed request from your security perf.
[00:09:10] [00:09:20] Maya: switching gears — i'll show the trace map visualization for a range of requests. so here's the "hop map" where each node is a service or model stage, edges are latencies, and color intensity is number of calls. this map quickly showed the reranker node as the hotspot.
[00:09:34] Omar: we also overlay errors and fallback events so you can see which model variants triggered fallbacks. see that little red badge on v2-q4_approx? that's the fallback frequency.
[00:09:45] Carlos: can we expose that fallback frequency to our alerting? like a metric we can scrape?
[00:09:49] Omar: yes, you can emit fallback.rate and fallback.latency metrics to Prometheus via the metrics exporter or forward to CloudWatch.
[00:09:58] [00:10:05] Priya: on data residency — some EU customers need traces never leave eu-west-1. is that possible?
[00:10:11] Elena: yes, for Private and Dedicated we can pin control plane and logs to region. hosted accounts can request region-scoped tenancy for logs; we'll detail options in the followup.
[00:10:21] Dana: competitor question — how do you compare with Anthropic or Vertex in terms of traceability tools?
[00:10:27] Maya: short answer: we focus on production debugging primitives — request replay, hop maps, and integrated rollout controls — lots of vendors have logs but fewer tie trace playback to model rollouts and automated fallback policies.
[00:10:39] [00:10:45] Carlos: any limitations we should be aware of?
[00:10:48] Omar: small ones — for the hosted tier the full prompt is redacted in exported artifacts by default, and very old traces beyond retention window need to be pulled from the raw storage. Also very high-cardinality traces may be sampled; we can lift sampling for specific routes in Dedicated.
[00:11:02] Maya: ok let's walk through a short live repro. Carlos you said you could reproduce with a small script?
[00:11:07] Carlos: yep i have a script that blasts 200 concurrent personalization requests — we'll run it for a minute and watch the console.
[00:11:13] [00:11:20] Carlos: starting load now...
[00:11:24] Omar: i'm watching the dashboard — i see queue build at minute 0:19, small spikes in queued requests then a couple of fallback events at 0:21. tokens cost per req also climbs.
[00:11:36] Maya: CPU on the model nodes looks okay but the queue latency is where we spike. can you show the request timeline for a sample retry?
[00:11:43] Omar: selecting a timed-out req, here's the retry cascade — client reties after 300ms with no jitter which amplified the burst. recommended: exponential backoff with jitter.
[00:11:55] Carlos: we currently use fixed backoff oof. okay we'll change that.
[00:11:59] [00:12:05] Aisha: while running load, is any PII leaving our VPC? we route through your public hosted api —
[00:12:12] Elena: for hosted flows it's out of your VPC, but we encrypt in transit and at rest; for strict regulated workloads we recommend Private or Dedicated w/ VPC peering.
[00:12:23] Priya: last question on the pilot: what's the SLA on Dedicated? we need 99.95 for serving.
[00:12:29] Maya: Dedicated SLA is 99.95 for the serving plane for the committed pool; we'll include the SLA terms in the contract doc.
[00:12:36] [00:12:40] Dana: ok good. any other quick feature asks?
[00:12:44] Carlos: it'd be helpful if the Console could auto-correlate our internal trace id when we push a header from kubernetes. currently we set X-Request-Id but sometimes the frontend rewrites it.
[00:12:55] Omar: we can ingest alternative headers — we'll add a note on how to make the header durable across proxies.
[00:13:02] Maya: recap before we close: 1) we'll send the incident export and trace map (Maya) 2) Elena will send security pack and KMS details (Elena) 3) Omar will spin up a small Dedicated trial and Optimize profile for the 72hr pilot (Omar) 4) Carlos will share the 3 request ids and the load script (Carlos) 5) schedule a pilot kickoff next week, tentatively 2027-05-18.
[00:13:26] [00:13:35] Dana: that works for us, thanks for the walkthrough — this was really practical.
[00:13:40] Maya: great, thanks everyone. we'll follow up with links: replay export, perf spreadsheet, SOC2 pack, and the Splunk connector runbook.
[00:13:50] Omar: also attaching sample curl for the warm-prefix API and the script to pin model variants.
[00:13:58] Carlos: appreciate it. bye.
[00:14:02] Maya: bye all.

Note: shared artifacts referenced during call: https://redwood.example.com/decks/retailbridge-incident-replay, benchmark sheet (shared drive) — "rb-pilot-bench-2027-05.xlsx". The transcript has the usual speech imperfections and occasional mislabels; speakers were sometimes talking over each other during load test.
